title: Hollis & Vane: closing the loss-making stores
prompt: A department store chain's accounts are built in two layers, and the difference between them decides most turnaround arguments. The first layer is what a store itself earns: its sales, less the cost of the goods it sells, less the payroll, rent and running costs of that building — its store contribution. The second layer is head office: buying, marketing, technology, finance and the executive team, whose cost is spread across the stores as an allocation. A store's reported profit is its contribution less that allocation, and the allocation does not disappear when the store does. Our client is Hollis & Vane, a chain of 120 stores with $2.4B of revenue, now losing money at group level, whose lenders have accepted a plan to reach $120M of EBIT within three years — an improvement of $180M from today's −$60M. A new CEO has been brought in to deliver it. Her board has fixed on the obvious first move: twenty stores report losses, and the board wants them closed. She has asked us to check the number before she commits to it, and to tell her what closing them would take out of an organisation that is already exhausted.

exhibits.title: Exhibit 1 — The two layers of a Hollis & Vane store P&L
exhibits.text: Store contribution = store sales − cost of goods sold − store payroll − rent − other local running costs. Reported store EBIT = store contribution − allocated head-office cost. Head-office cost is allocated to stores in proportion to their sales. Closing a store removes its contribution immediately; it removes head-office cost only to the extent that head office actually shrinks.

exhibits.title: Exhibit 2 — Hollis & Vane, annual figures

rows: EBIT improvement the lenders' plan requires

exhibits.unitsNote: Head-office cost is allocated across stores in proportion to sales.

exhibits.title: Exhibit 3 — The twenty weakest stores, per store per year (Scenario 1)

rows: Share of the allocated head-office cost that head office would genuinely remove if the store closed
One-off severance and lease exit cost if the store closes

exhibits.unitsNote: $M per store per year, except the two marked otherwise. All twenty stores are close enough to this average to be treated as identical. Leases on these twenty can be exited within the year at the cost shown.
exhibits.source: Store-level management accounts and the property team

exhibits.title: Exhibit 4 — Scenario 2: the head-office reduction is happening anyway

rows: Share of the allocated head-office cost that head office would genuinely remove if the store closed
One-off severance and lease exit cost if the store closes

exhibits.unitsNote: Changed from Scenario 1: the board has already committed to its head-office reduction and will deliver it whether or not the stores close, so no further head-office cost comes out with them. Every other figure is unchanged.

questions.prompt: Let's start with the right structure. What are the three key questions you would need to answer before the CEO commits to closing the twenty stores? Please summarise them in 3 lines maximum.

keyPoints: What do these stores actually earn or lose before head-office allocation — is the reported loss a store problem or an accounting one?
What genuinely goes away if they close: which costs are avoidable, what happens to their sales, and what does the exit cost up front?
What does closing them cost the organisation — who leaves, who is left to run the change, and can the same team deliver the rest of the $180M?
commonMistakes: A generic turnaround framework rather than the three questions this specific decision turns on.
Accepting the board's premise that a reported loss means a value-destroying store.
Leaving out the people dimension entirely, when the CEO has asked about it directly.
Naming six things when the interviewer asked for three.

questions.followUp: Good. The finance team has pulled the store-level detail, and the property team has priced the exits. Note the second-to-last line: the allocation and what head office would actually remove are not the same number.

questions.prompt: Scenario 1: given the data in the exhibits, what would closing all twenty stores do to Hollis & Vane's annual EBIT? Please give your answer rounded to the nearest whole number, without further explanation or working.
questions.answerFormatNote: Give your answer in USD per year, rounded to the nearest whole number (for example 1111 or 123456 or 500885), without further explanation or working. If EBIT would fall, enter the answer with a minus sign, for example -250000.

idealAnswer.workedSolution:
Store contribution, per store: sales $10.0M − cost of goods $6.0M − payroll $2.4M − rent $1.0M − other local costs $0.4M = $0.2M. Positive: these stores cover their own costs and contribute $0.2M each.
Their reported loss of $1.05M each comes entirely from the $1.25M of head-office cost allocated to them.
Closing all twenty removes 20 × $0.2M = $4.0M of contribution.
Head office genuinely shrinks by 40% of the allocated cost: 20 × $1.25M × 40% = $10.0M.
Annual EBIT impact = −$4.0M + $10.0M = +$6,000,000 a year.
There is also a one-off cost of 20 × $2.0M = $40M, and the board's assumption — that closing stores reporting $1.05M losses each saves $21M a year — is wrong by more than three times.
keyPoints: A reported store loss driven by allocation is not a cash loss; the store contribution is what closing actually removes.
Allocated cost only goes away to the extent head office actually shrinks — here 40 cents in the dollar.
The move is worth $6M against a $180M plan: real, but not the centrepiece the board thinks it is.
commonMistakes: Taking the reported losses at face value and answering $21,000,000.
Removing the whole allocated cost and answering $21,000,000 by a different route — 20 × ($1.25M − $0.2M).
Netting the $40M one-off into an annual figure.
Treating the stores' sales as lost profit rather than working from contribution.

questions.prompt: Please explain briefly the reasoning behind your answer to the previous question, in 3 lines maximum.

keyPoints: These stores are not losing money at store level: each contributes $0.2M after every cost the building itself incurs.
The reported loss is an allocation of head-office cost, and that cost only leaves the business if head office is actually made smaller.
So closing them removes real contribution and saves only the 40% of allocation head office would genuinely take out, netting about $6M a year.
It is worth doing, but it is a small part of a $180M plan, and it costs $40M up front to get.
commonMistakes: Explaining the arithmetic without naming the difference between contribution and allocated cost.
Saying the stores are profitable without qualifying that this is before head office.
Not putting the answer in the context of the $180M the plan needs.

questions.followUp: Understood. For context, the average Hollis & Vane store turns over $20M a year, so these twenty are half the size of the chain's average — which is how they came to look like the problem.

questions.prompt: I'd like to check a couple of the parameters behind that. How much store contribution would Hollis & Vane give up in a year by closing all twenty? Please give your answer rounded to the nearest whole number, without further explanation or working.
questions.answerFormatNote: Give your answer in USD per year, rounded to the nearest whole number (for example 1111 or 123456 or 500885), without further explanation or working.

idealAnswer.workedSolution:
Per store: $10.0M − $6.0M − $2.4M − $1.0M − $0.4M = $0.2M of contribution.
Twenty stores: 20 × $0.2M = $4,000,000 a year.
keyPoints: Contribution stops at the store's own costs; the allocation is not one of them.
The figure is positive, which is the whole point of asking.
commonMistakes: Including the allocated head-office cost and answering −$21,000,000.
Using gross margin only and answering $80,000,000.
Answering $200,000,000, the sales rather than the contribution.

questions.followUp: Thanks. The finance director confirms the allocation is formulaic — head office is spread across stores by sales, and no part of it was ever charged to a store because that store caused it.

questions.prompt: And how much head-office cost would genuinely come out of the business in a year if all twenty closed? Please give your answer rounded to the nearest whole number, without further explanation or working.
questions.answerFormatNote: Give your answer in USD per year, rounded to the nearest whole number (for example 1111 or 123456 or 500885), without further explanation or working.

idealAnswer.workedSolution:
Allocated head-office cost across the twenty = 20 × $1.25M = $25.0M.
Head office would genuinely remove 40% of it: $25.0M × 40% = $10,000,000 a year.
The other $15.0M is redistributed across the remaining 100 stores, making each of them look slightly worse without anything having changed.
keyPoints: Avoidable cost, not allocated cost, is what a closure decision runs on.
The unavoidable 60% does not vanish — it lands on the stores that remain.
commonMistakes: Answering $25,000,000 by removing the whole allocation.
Applying the 40% to the store contribution instead of the allocated cost.
Answering $300,000,000, the whole head-office cost.

questions.followUp: That redistribution matters more than it sounds: it is how a chain talks itself into closing a second tranche of stores next year. Before we move on, the CEO wants to know how robust the $6M is.

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements, if true, would change the annual EBIT impact you calculated? Select all that apply.
options: One pound in every five of a closed store's sales transfers to another Hollis & Vane store, at the same gross margin and with no extra cost in the receiving store
The leases on the twenty stores have four years left and cannot be exited early: the rent must be paid until they expire
Two of the twenty stores are freehold and could be sold for $12M each
A competitor has announced it will close fifteen stores in the same towns
Each of the twenty stores reports a loss of $1.05M a year after head-office allocation

optionRationale: Changes it, and by more than anything else on this list. A fifth of $10M is $2M of sales moving to a store that keeps 40% of it with no extra cost: $0.8M per closed store, $16M across the twenty, taking the annual impact to $22M. Transfer is the single most important number in any store-closure case, and it is the one the board did not mention.

Changes it. Rent of $1.0M a store would carry on being paid, so each closure gives up $1.2M rather than $0.2M: $24M of cost against $10M of head-office saving, and the annual impact becomes −$14M. Whether a cost is avoidable is a question about the contract, not about the accounts.

Does not change the annual EBIT impact. $24M of proceeds is real money and belongs in the cash case for closing — but it is a one-off receipt, not a change to the annual run rate you were asked about.
Does not change it. It may well be a reason to keep the stores open and take the competitor's customers, which makes it worth raising — but nothing in your calculation moves because of it.
Does not change it. That is the exhibit restated, and that reported loss is exactly the figure the analysis has just shown to be misleading.
keyPoints: Sort each statement into: does it change the contribution lost, the cost avoided, or neither?
One-off cash and annual run rate are different questions; a closure case needs both, separately.
A cost is avoidable only if a contract lets you stop paying it.
commonMistakes: Picking the freehold sale because $24M is a big number, without noticing it is a one-off.
Missing the lease term, which is the difference between a $6M gain and a $14M loss.
Missing the transfer of sales, which is the first thing an experienced retailer would ask about.

questions.followUp: The CEO has taken both points. There is also a development at board level: the head-office reduction she was planning has now been committed to publicly, on its own timetable.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is likely to be true for Scenario 2 compared with Scenario 1? Use the data below for your revised calculation. The change is described under the exhibit.
options: Closing the twenty stores now reduces annual EBIT
The gain is smaller but closing the stores still improves EBIT
The impact is unchanged, because the stores' own economics have not moved
There is not enough information to decide

optionRationale: Correct. If head office shrinks anyway, none of that saving is caused by the closures. All that is left is the contribution given up: −$4,000,000 a year, plus the $40M one-off. The stores were only ever 'loss-making' because of a cost the company is now removing without touching them.
Wrong. There is no saving left to set against the lost contribution — the whole $10M was the head-office reduction, which is now happening regardless.

Wrong. The stores' own economics are indeed unchanged, which is exactly why the answer changes: the entire benefit of closing them came from somewhere else, and that somewhere else has been claimed by another decision.
Wrong. The exhibit changes one line and holds the rest. Worth choosing where something is genuinely missing; here nothing is.
keyPoints: +$6M becomes −$4M, and nothing about the stores changed.

A saving that another decision is already delivering cannot be counted again here — that is double counting across two workstreams, and it is how turnaround plans come to promise more than they deliver.
The stores are worth keeping on these numbers; the head-office reduction is worth doing on its own merits.
commonMistakes: Re-deriving the store contribution, which has not moved.
Assuming a smaller saving must still be a saving.
Choosing 'not enough information' because the board's commitment sounds like it needs more detail.

questions.prompt: Please explain in 2 to 3 lines the reasoning behind your answer to the previous question — and say what you would now tell the CEO to do about the twenty stores.

keyPoints: The benefit of closing was never in the stores; it was the head-office cost that came out alongside them, and another decision now claims that saving.
On these numbers closing destroys $4M a year and costs $40M to do, so the recommendation is to stop the closure programme, not to shrink it.
Keep the stores under review on contribution rather than on reported EBIT, and revisit any store whose contribution turns negative or whose lease comes up.

A strong answer adds that the $180M has to be found somewhere else, and that management attention is itself scarce — the closure programme would have consumed the team for a year for less than 4% of the plan.
commonMistakes: Recommending a partial closure without a reason why some stores differ.
Explaining what changed in the exhibit rather than what the CEO should now do.
Missing that the real cost of the wrong decision is the organisation's attention, which is the CEO's actual constraint.

questions.followUp: That is the message she needs to take back to her board. The head-office reduction is still going ahead, and she has asked for help sizing it properly.

questions.prompt: Choose the four pieces of data that, when combined, would allow us to estimate the five-year net saving from a voluntary redundancy programme in head office.
options: Number of roles leaving in each year of the programme
Average salary and employment on-costs of a leaving role
One-off severance cost per leaving role
Cost of contractors and backfill in each year of the programme
Average length of service of the leavers
Share of leavers who go voluntarily rather than compulsorily
Notice period each leaving role must serve

optionRationale: Needed. The saving builds as people leave, so the profile by year is what drives it.
Needed. Salary alone understates a role: pension, national insurance and benefits go with it.
Needed. Severance is the price of the saving, and it lands before the saving arrives.
Needed, and the most commonly forgotten: work does not disappear with the person, and backfill is what turns a headline saving into a real one.
Not needed. Length of service is what drives severance, and the severance cost per role is already on the list — take both and you have spent a pick on the input to another input.
Not needed for the same reason. Voluntary and compulsory exits cost different amounts, and that difference is already inside the severance cost per role.
Not needed. Notice periods decide when in the year a saving starts, and the year-by-year profile of leavers already carries the phasing.
keyPoints: Five-year net saving = Σ over years of (roles gone by that year × salary and on-costs − backfill cost) − severance paid.
That expression consumes exactly the four selected items and nothing else.
Three of the wrong options are inputs to inputs: they are already inside a figure you have picked.
commonMistakes: Taking length of service because redundancy pay obviously depends on it.
Leaving out backfill, which is what makes head-office reductions under-deliver.
Taking the notice period, which affects timing the leaver profile already captures.

questions.followUp: Thanks. One last thing before we write this up.

questions.prompt: Your BCG project leader has asked what the turnaround will cost Hollis & Vane as an organisation — the people and capability risks the CEO has to manage while delivering $180M. Could you share your thoughts in 3 to 4 lines?

keyPoints: The best people leave first: strong performers have options, and a year of announced redundancies is when they use them — the ones you most need to deliver the plan are the ones most able to go.
Middle management carries both jobs at once, running the stores and delivering the change, and there is no slack left after a head-office reduction.
Capability loss: cutting head office by role rather than by capability strips out buying and merchandising skill the recovery depends on.
Change fatigue and rumour reach the shop floor and then the customer — service is the product in a department store.

Credibility: announcing a store-closure programme and then reversing it, as this analysis implies, costs the CEO something with her board and her staff unless she frames the reversal as evidence the plan is being tested properly.
commonMistakes: Listing generic change-management risks with no link to how this business runs.
Missing that attention and capability, not cash, are the binding constraints in a turnaround.
Repeating the store-closure conclusion instead of naming organisational risks.

closing: That is everything I wanted to cover. You went behind the reported store losses to what the stores actually contribute, separated the head-office cost that would genuinely leave from the cost that would simply be redistributed, and then found that another decision had already claimed the saving. Thank you — the CEO takes this to her board on Thursday.
